'''Xu Ruiyun''' ({{lang-zh|s=徐瑞云}}; 15 June 1915{{spnd}}23 January 1969), also known as '''Süe-Yung Zee-Kiang''',{{efn|"Kiang" is the romanization of her husband's last name Jiang (江).}} was a [[Chinese mathematician]] specialising in [[mathematical analysis]]. A student of [[Constantin Carathéodory]], she was the first Chinese woman to receive a [[doctorate]] in mathematics. In 1941, she returned to China and worked at [[Zhejiang University]] and later [[Hangzhou University]]. In 1969, during the [[Cultural Revolution]], she died by suicide.

== Biography ==
Xu was born in [[Shanghai]] on 15 June 1915. Her family originally came from [[Cixi, Zhejiang]]. Her father was an industrialist who owned a factory making socks. In 1927, she entered [[Wu Pen Girls' School]].{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|p=74}} In 1932 she entered [[Zhejiang University]] in [[Hangzhou]], where she studied under [[Chen Jiangong]] and [[Su Buqing]].{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|p=75}} She graduated in 1936 and was hired as a teaching assistant.{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|p=76}} At Zhejiang University she also entered a relationship with biology student [[Jiang Ximing]]. They married in February 1937.{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|p=76}}

In 1937, Xu and Jiang received the Humboldt scholarship to study in [[Nazi Germany|Germany]]. They left China in May 1937, were delayed for a month and a half in [[Milan]], before arriving in Germany in August.{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|pages=76–77}} They first studied the German language in [[Berlin]] for two months, and then entered the [[Doctor of Philosophy|PhD]] program at the [[Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München]].{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|p=77}} Xu was supervised by [[Constantin Carathéodory]] and studied [[trigonometric series]], in particular [[Fourier series]].{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|p=77}} At the end of 1940, she received her doctorate, becoming the first Chinese woman PhD in mathematics.{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|p=77}}{{sfn|Xu|2015|p=46}}{{sfn|Xue|Liu|Peng|2020|p=527}}

In January 1941, Xu and Jiang left Germany. In March, they arrived in [[Chongqing]], the wartime capital of China during the [[Second Sino-Japanese War]]. In April, they arrived in [[Meitan County|Meitan, Guizhou]], where the College of Science of Zhejiang University held its wartime campus.{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|pages=77–78}} There she lectured in mathematics, and her students included {{ill|Cao Xihua|zh|曹锡华}}, {{ill|Ye Yanqian|zh|叶彦谦}}, and some later Chinese mathematicians.{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|p=78}} After the end of the war, Xu was promoted to professor in 1946, when she was 31. She returned to Hangzhou with Zhejiang University in the same year.{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|p=79}}

The [[People's Republic of China]] was established in 1949. During the [[1952 reorganisation of Chinese higher education]], Xu remained at Zhejiang University, where she was the office director of teaching and research in higher mathematics. Around this time she joined the [[China Democratic League]] and studied [[communism]].{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|p=80}} In 1953 she was moved to Zhejiang Teachers College ({{lang-zh|浙江师范学院}}, later became [[Hangzhou University]] in 1958), where she chaired the department of mathematics.{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|pages=80–81}} During her time at Zhejiang Teachers College, she learned Russian and translated [[Isidor Natanson]]'s ''Theory of Functions of a Real Variable'', which was published in Chinese in 1955.{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|p=82}}

Around this time, Xu was elected as a representative to the [[Zhejiang Provincial People's Congress]] in 1954 and a member of the {{ill|People's Government of Zhejiang|zh|浙江省人民政府}}. She was also elected as the secretary general of the Zhejiang Mathematical Society (浙江省数学会). In 1956, Xu joined the [[Chinese Communist Party]].{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|pages=82–83}}

In 1964, Xu and [[Hua Luogeng]] chaired the first national conference on functional analysis at the [[Hengshan Picardie Hotel|Hengshan Hotel]] in Shanghai. She was the CCP [[party group]] leader at the conference. In 1965, Xu began to translate Carathéodory's ''Theory of Functions of a Complex Variable''. She could not complete it due to her workload in the [[Socialist Education Movement]].{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|pages=86–87}} After the [[Cultural Revolution]] began in 1966, Xu began to undergo [[struggle session]]s within Hangzhou University. She was forced to kneel for long times and was whipped. In 1968, Xu's husband Jiang Ximing was accused of being a German spy, and Xu was detained and was [[Forced confession|pressured to confess]] her alleged spy activities. On 23 January 1969, Xu committed [[suicide by hanging]].{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|pages=87–89}}

In 1978, Hangzhou University held a commemoration ceremony and [[Political rehabilitation|rehabilitated]] Xu. She was buried in {{ill|Liuxia Subdistrict|zh|留下街道}}, Hangzhou.{{sfn|Zhao|1999b|p=89}} In 2009, the department of mathematics of Zhejiang University purchased a new grave for Xu and made a new tombstone.{{sfn|Xu|2015|p=47}} On 13 June 2015, Zhejiang University held a conference commemorating the 100th anniversary of Xu's birth.{{sfn|Xu|2015|p=45}}

== Works and influences ==

Xue et al. consider Xu to be a member of the third generation of the mathematical analysis tradition at Zhejiang University.{{sfn|Xue|Liu|Peng|2020|p=524}} Xu's publications include:
* {{cite journal|journal=Mathematische Zeitschrift  |title=Über die Fouriersche Entwicklung der singulären Funktion bei einer Lebesgueschen Zerlegung
 |first=Süe-Yung |last=Kiang |date=18 January 1941 |publication-date=December 1942 |doi=10.1007/BF01180966 |volume=47 |pages=330–342}}{{efn|Some sources consider this work Xu's PhD dissertation.{{sfn|Xue|Liu|Peng|2020|p=523}}}}
* {{cite journal|journal=Journal of the London Mathematical Society |title=On the Variation of Increasing Functions Whose First ''2n'' Fourier Coefficients are Given |first=Süe-Yung |last=Zee-Kiang |date=April 1944 |doi=10.1112/jlms/19.74_Part_2.71 |volume=19 |issue=74|pages=71–77 }}

Xu's translations include:
* {{cite book|script-title=zh:实变函数论 |trans-title=Theory of Functions of a Real Variable |first=Isidor |last=Natanson |language=zh |translator-first=Ruiyun |translator-last=Xu |editor-first=Jiangong |editor-last=Chen |orig-date=1955 |edition=5 |publication-date=2010 |isbn=9787040292213}}
* {{cite book|script-title=zh:富里埃级数 |trans-title=Fourier Series |first1=G. H. |last1=Hardy |author-link=G. H. Hardy |first2=W. W. |last2=Rogosinski |author-link2=Werner Wolfgang Rogosinski|translator1= Xu, Ruiyun |translator2 = Wang, Silei |orig-date= 1956|publication-date=1978}}

When she was teaching at Zhejiang University, Xu was the thesis advisor of the Chinese American mathematician [[Yuan-Shih Chow]].{{sfn|Ying|Zhang|2006|loc = "Ruiyun Xu, a student of Carathéodory, directed my thesis. She wrote an excellent book on real variables and later became Chairwoman of the Department of Mathematics at Hangzhou University}} Three members of the [[Chinese Academy of Sciences]]–[[Shi Zhongci]], [[Wang Yuan (mathematician)|Wang Yuan]], and [[Hu Hesheng]]–had taken her classes at the university.{{sfn|Zhang|2015}} Her adopted daughter also became a PhD in mathematics.{{sfn|Zhang|2015}}
